chunks: Inductor at t = 0⁺ and DC steady state. The question: How does an inductor behave when initially excited and at DC steady-state?
An inductor is a coil of wire that resists changes in the current through it.
Right after you switch a voltage on, the current in the coil is still zero and cannot jump, so the coil acts like a gap in the wire.
After a long time the current is steady, and an ideal coil acts like a plain piece of wire.
Picture a heavy merry-go-round. At the first push it barely moves. Once it spins steadily, it needs almost no push to keep going.
The coil's current is the spin speed, and the voltage across it is the push.
The analogy breaks in one place: a real coil's wire has a little resistance, like a bit of friction, so it never drops exactly zero volts.
The switch closes at t = 0 with the inductor de-energized. The node voltage v x is also the inductor voltage.
Inductor: a coil of wire that stores energy in a magnetic field. Open circuit: a break in the path. No current flows, but voltage can appear across it.
Short circuit: a plain wire. Current flows freely and there is zero voltage across it.
DC steady state: the condition after all the switching is over and nothing is changing anymore.
Current cannot jump: an inductor's current is the same just after a switch as just before it.
Time constant ( tau ): the time the current takes to make most (about 63%) of its change, equal to L over R .
Connect a 10 volts source through a 10 ohms resistor to an inductor, and close the switch.
At that instant the inductor current is 0 amps, so the inductor is open and has the full 10 volts across it. Much later, the current stops changing and the inductor drops 0 volts.
All 10 volts is across the resistor, so the current is 10 volts / 10 ohms = 1 amps. That is the whole idea.
"When first excited from zero current, an inductor acts like an open circuit: its current can't jump, so it's still zero right after the step and the full voltage appears across it.
At DC steady state it's a short, because constant current means L di over dt equals 0 ; a real one shows just its DC resistance.
In between, the current rises exponentially with tau equals L over R . If it was already carrying current, at the switch instant it acts as a current source.
It's the dual of a capacitor."
